**The non-answer worth noting.** Jefferies' Mistry, twice, tried to get Streichert to bless the EUR 1.9 billion 2025 consensus. He declined both times. In hindsight the actual ~EUR 1.96 billion means he *would* have been right to bless it — his refusal was discipline, not evasion.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

**🔴 Red flags**

- **The bottom line has gone backwards for three years while the narrative went forwards.** Net income 1.67B → 1.38B → 1.34B (2023–2025); earnings per share 1.40 → 1.15 → 1.12. Every call in this set was delivered against a *falling* earnings trend. (All five quarters.)
- **Free cash flow is negative and structurally so.** Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow −EUR 390 million; capital spending 1.92× depreciation. The fleet programme management sells as the future is the reason the present generates no cash. (Q3-25, Q4-25 fleet discussion vs financials.)
- **A dividend raised 10% out of negative free cash flow**, with a solvency score in the distress band (Altman Z 1.2) and a 30% payout ratio computed on earnings that are themselves declining. (Q4-25.)
- **The rolling "transition year."** Three consecutive years in which the clean year is next year. (Q1-25, Q2-25, Q3-25, Q4-25.)
- **Headline unit revenue is flattered by non-ticket items** — ancillaries, cargo belly and irregularity-cost relief are all inside the reported RASK. (Q3-25, Streichert.)
- **Structural handicaps are now permanent narrative furniture**: Russian airspace, EU regulation, German location costs. Management has, in effect, told the market its ceiling is set by third parties. (Q2-25 onward.)
- **Persistent overstaffing conceded**, with efficiency deferred past 2026. (Q1-25, Spohr to Bernstein.)

**🟢 Green flags**

- **Operational turnaround delivered and quantified**: regularity 99%, punctuality +10 points, irregularity cost −43% / EUR 362 million. This is the rarest thing in a turnaround — a promise made, kept, and measured in euros. (Q3-25, Q4-25.)
- **Candour about failure.** The 2024 miss was volunteered, attributed (95% to the core brand), and not spun. The Middle East hit was raised by the chief executive unprompted. (Q4-24, Q4-25.)
- **The non-airline portfolio genuinely works.** Technik EUR 635 million (record) and Cargo EUR 251 million in 2024, with the group earning EUR 1.6 billion "without a single euro contribution from the core airline." The multi-brand, multi-hub structure is validated, not merely asserted. (Q4-24.)
- **Allegris is producing measurable pricing power**: "12% higher yields for Allegris than for the former business class," ancillaries +15% in 2025, with only 10 of ~200 wide-bodies converted at mid-2025 — a long runway that is arithmetic, not hope. (Q2-25, Q4-25.)
- **Guidance discipline improved** from "double-digit" hand-waving to explicit margin, free-cash-flow and capital-spending figures.
- **Accounting quality is high** (Piotroski 8/9); revenue at a record EUR 39.6 billion; book value per share compounding at 12.7% over five years.
- **ITA was accretive earlier than promised** — "earlier than expected, we see positive financial effects from our investment in ITA already in the second quarter," with the 41% stake contributing EUR 90 million of net income in 2025. (Q2-25, Q4-25.)

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The capital-allocation vocabulary hardened — and it is the most important shift in the set.** In October 2025 Spohr answered a routine capacity question with an unusually disciplined formulation: "since coming out of COVID, beyond operational requirements, we really allocate aircraft and growth according to ROCE principle. So where do we return investments highest?" He then named the beneficiaries — Discover, Edelweiss, Lufthansa City Airlines, ITA — every one of them a *lower-cost* platform, and none of them the core Lufthansa mainline. He added that this is "also internally clearly communicated to unions, to our staff."

Read plainly: **Lufthansa is systematically starving its own flag carrier of growth and redirecting it to cheaper labour platforms, and is saying so publicly to pressure the unions.** The April 2025 call made the mechanism explicit — the 2023 pilots' contract "allows us unlimited growth in Lufthansa City Airlines and in Discover… they decided in '23 to rather go for high salary increases. And on the other hand, for that, we got the freedom to use growth in those airlines." This is a slow, contractual, structural cost fix that does not depend on winning a fight. It is the single most underappreciated positive in these transcripts.

**"Transition year" is doing load-bearing work.** The phrase is not decoration; it is the mechanism by which a three-year earnings decline is presented as progress.

**Competition talk shifted from carriers to states.** Early calls benchmark against airlines. Later calls benchmark against jurisdictions — Gulf carriers' airspace access, EU regulation, German taxation. Management's competitive frame has moved from "we can beat them" to "the playing field is tilted."

**A quiet geographic re-basing.** "Second largest intercontinental area for Lufthansa is not anymore China but by now India" (Q4-25), alongside an Air India partnership. China was dropped without ceremony.

**The tariff reversal is a real, unmodelled positive.** In Q4-25 Spohr noted the US tariffs that cost Technik roughly EUR 20 million in the first half of 2025 "have been ruled illegal by the Supreme Court. So at least they don't go forward. Probably there will also be reimbursements." A margin headwind is becoming a possible one-off tailwind.

**One voice, one message.** No management change across the period; Spohr and Streichert have been consistent and mutually reinforcing. There is no new voice saying anything different — which removes a common source of narrative drift, and also removes any fresh perspective.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE.**

Not STRENGTHENING, despite a strong temptation to call it that. The operational recovery is genuine, measured and delivered — but it has now run for six quarters without reaching the bottom line. Net income has fallen three years running, earnings per share is down 2.6% year-on-year, free cash flow is negative, and return on invested capital is 0.4%. A turnaround that improves adjusted operating profit by 19% while the owner's earnings decline is not yet strengthening the enterprise; it is offsetting the cost of the fleet transition. Not DETERIORATING either — revenue is at a record, accounting quality is high, the balance sheet is stressed but not breaking, and the operational fix is real.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing a position:**

**Every euro of the operational recovery is currently being consumed by the fleet programme, and the company is paying a rising dividend out of negative free cash flow while carrying EUR 5.32 billion of net debt and an Altman Z-score of 1.2.** The bull case is not "does the turnaround work" — it demonstrably is working operationally. The bull case is "does the turnaround out-earn the capital intensity before the balance sheet or the cycle forces a choice." Management's own answer is that 2026 still carries transitional drag and 2027 is the first clean year — while a EUR 1.7 billion fuel headwind lands in 2026 and a Gulf conflict remains unresolved. The director is not underwriting an operational thesis. The director is underwriting a *cash-conversion* thesis, on a levered balance sheet, into a live oil shock, with the company's own guidance putting the payoff a year beyond the current fiscal year.

**Economic moat: NARROW.**

The moat type is a *regulatory-license and scale-cost* hybrid: slot portfolios at Frankfurt, Munich and Zurich; a six-hub European network; the Miles & More loyalty franchise; the North Atlantic joint venture with United and Air Canada (an antitrust-immunised structure that is genuinely hard to replicate); and, distinctly, Lufthansa Technik's intangible/scale position in a global MRO market management sizes at roughly USD 100 billion a year with a structural aging-fleet tailwind.

The width judgement is set by the returns evidence, not the asset list. **Return on invested capital of 0.4% and return on equity of 0.2% are far below any plausible cost of capital**, gross margin is 9.5% and contracting, and net margin is 3.4%. A business earning 0.4% on invested capital does not have a wide moat regardless of how attractive its slots are. But the returns are *low from a rebuilt base*, not *high and falling*: book value per share has compounded at 12.7% over five years, adjusted operating profit rose 19% in 2025, and the company is emerging from a 2021 loss of EUR 2.19 billion. That is the signature of a narrow moat at a cyclical and transitional low, not an eroding one.

**Moat trend: STABLE.** Two forces offset. Eroding it: the Russian-airspace handicap versus Gulf and Chinese carriers is a genuine, unrecoverable structural cost disadvantage on Asian routes; European regulatory and location costs rise on a one-way ratchet; Ryanair, Wizz and easyJet continue to compress short-haul economics. Widening it: the low-cost-platform migration (Discover, City Airlines, Edelweiss, ITA) is contractually secured and permanent; Allegris is demonstrating 12% pricing uplift with roughly 95% of the wide-body fleet still unconverted; Technik grows above a market compounding at 2–3%; and the ITA majority acquisition adds a sixth hub and doubles Latin American reach. Net: stable.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE — and the cheapness is neither a clean fear-print nor a value trap.**

No structural force threatens aviation's terminal value. The demand curve is the opposite of secular decline: management cites IATA's forecast that global passenger numbers double over the next 20 years against constrained aircraft supply — "strong demand growth meets limited supply very likely for many years to come." None of the recognised terminal-impairment forces applies here. Artificial intelligence does not displace physical travel; the videoconferencing thesis was tested to destruction in 2020–2021 and premium long-haul demand is now running ahead of economy on Lufthansa's own data ("first class is even going better than business class, business class is going better than premium economy"). The energy transition is a cost and regulatory drag on aviation, not a demand-displacement force — there is no substitute technology for long-haul flight on any relevant horizon.

The honest characterisation of the discount is therefore neither of the two clean answers. It is **a deserved quality discount, not a mispricing**. Lufthansa is cheap on book-value and Graham measures precisely because it converts almost none of its record revenue into owner cash: negative free cash flow, 0.4% return on invested capital, a distress-zone solvency score, and a cost structure that is politically and contractually hard to move. That is not the market pricing in terminal decline against stable earnings power — the earnings power genuinely is impaired today, by the company's own admission, through at least 2026. The base is cyclical and recovering, not melting; but the market is not making an error that requires correcting. It is charging a fair price for a low-return, high-capital-intensity, geopolitically-levered business that happens to own two genuinely good assets (Technik and the hub/joint-venture franchise) inside a mediocre one.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 4 | TRAJECTORY: STABLE | MOAT: NARROW | MOAT_TREND: STABLE | SECULAR_THREAT: manageable

bull_thesis:
The bull case is that Lufthansa is a genuinely successful operational turnaround that the market is still pricing as a broken airline, and that two good businesses are trapped inside the valuation of a mediocre one.

Start with what has actually been delivered. Management promised operational stability first and financial recovery second, and the operational half is done and measured in euros: network regularity at 99%, departure punctuality up more than 10 percentage points (third quarter of 2025), and flight-irregularity costs down 43% in 2025 — 'equivalent of EUR 362 million' (full-year 2025 call, March 2026). That is not a narrative; it is a cash line item. It carried adjusted operating profit (adjusted EBIT — profit before one-off items, the measure the company steers on) up roughly 19% in 2025 to about EUR 1.96 billion on record revenue of EUR 39.6 billion, up 5.4% year on year.

Second, the non-airline portfolio is genuinely good and genuinely undervalued inside the group. In 2024 Lufthansa Technik, the maintenance, repair and overhaul arm (MRO), earned a record EUR 635 million and Lufthansa Cargo EUR 251 million — such that the group made EUR 1.6 billion, in chief executive Carsten Spohr's words, 'without a single euro contribution from the core airline.' Technik sits in a market management sizes at roughly USD 100 billion a year, structurally growing 2-3% on aging global fleets, and it is targeting a 10% margin by 2030. The 2025 margin dip was tariff-driven, and that headwind is reversing: Spohr noted in March 2026 that the tariffs which cost Technik about EUR 20 million in the first half of 2025 'have been ruled illegal by the Supreme Court… Probably there will also be reimbursements.' A standalone Technik would not be valued at an airline multiple.

Third, there is a real, contractually-secured cost fix running in the background that requires winning no fight. Spohr said in October 2025 that capacity is allocated 'according to ROCE principle' — return on capital employed — and named the beneficiaries: Discover, Edelweiss, Lufthansa City Airlines, ITA. All are lower-cost platforms; none is the expensive mainline. The mechanism was made explicit in April 2025: the 2023 pilots' contract 'allows us unlimited growth in Lufthansa City Airlines and in Discover… they decided in '23 to rather go for high salary increases. And on the other hand, for that, we got the freedom to use growth in those airlines.' Lufthansa is lawfully and permanently migrating growth to cheaper labour, and telling the unions so.

Fourth, pricing power is arriving and is mostly still ahead. The new Allegris premium cabin is achieving '12% higher yields… than for the former business class' (March 2026), with ancillary revenue — fees for bags, seats and upgrades — up 15% in 2025. At mid-2025 only about 10 of roughly 200 wide-bodies carried Allegris. The runway here is arithmetic, not hope. Demand mix supports it: 'first class is even going better than business class, business class is going better than premium economy, and premium economy better than economy' (August 2025).

Fifth, the demand backdrop is structurally favourable and rare: IATA projects global passenger numbers double over 20 years against constrained aircraft supply — 'strong demand growth meets limited supply very likely for many years to come' (October 2025).

Conditions that must hold: (1) the EUR 1.5 billion gross turnaround contribution guided for 2026, rising to EUR 2.5 billion by 2028, actually lands; (2) 2026 free cash flow reaches the guided ~EUR 0.9 billion, turning the cash story positive; (3) the EUR 1.7 billion 2026 fuel headwind is absorbed without breaking the guided mid-single-digit margin; (4) fleet capital spending peaks near the guided ~EUR 2.9 billion and then falls, letting adjusted profit finally reach the bottom line; (5) no escalation of the Gulf conflict beyond the ten destinations already closed. If those hold, a business earning EUR 2.5-3.0 billion of adjusted operating profit with falling capital intensity, carrying a crown-jewel MRO asset and a sixth hub in Italy, is not a EUR 11 billion company.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is simpler and, on today's evidence, better supported: this is a business that converts a record top line into nothing for its owners, and the market is charging a fair price for that fact rather than making a mistake.

The decisive number is not adjusted operating profit. It is net income, and it has fallen for three consecutive years: EUR 1.67 billion (2023), EUR 1.38 billion (2024), EUR 1.34 billion (2025). Earnings per share tracked it down — 1.40, then 1.15, then 1.12, down 2.6% year on year — across exactly the period in which management was describing a successful turnaround. Both things are true at once, and the reason is mechanical: adjusted EBIT sits above the depreciation and interest thrown off by the record fleet programme that management calls its strategic centrepiece. Move one line down the income statement and 'up 19%' becomes 'down for three straight years.' Only one of those is in the headline.

The cash position is worse than the profit position. Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is negative EUR 390 million. Capital spending runs at 1.92 times depreciation and 109% of operating cash flow — the company is spending more than it earns from operations. Four of the five valuation models in our own scan (discounted cash flow, earnings power value, owner earnings, and the 15% intrinsic-value model) return negative margins of safety, because you cannot discount cash flows that do not exist. Only Graham's book-based method shows a discount, and book value is exactly the wrong lens for a business earning 0.4% on invested capital and 0.2% on equity. Cheapness measured against assets that generate no return is not value.

The balance sheet does not give this thesis time. Net debt is EUR 5.32 billion (excluding leases: EUR 13.02 billion of borrowings against EUR 7.70 billion of cash, at 31 March 2026). The Altman Z-score — a standard solvency composite — is 1.2, inside the distress zone. Working capital is negative EUR 4.2 billion and the current ratio is 0.81. Against that, management raised the dividend 10% to EUR 0.33 per share out of negative free cash flow. That is a choice to pay shareholders with borrowed money while funding the largest fleet renewal in company history.

The 2026 set-up is actively hostile. Management has guided to an incremental EUR 1.7 billion fuel bill for 2026 following the Gulf spike, with only 80-83% of passenger-airline fuel hedged — a hedge that still admits EUR 1.7 billion of damage is a speed bump, not a shield. Ten destinations were closed as of the March 2026 call, at a stated EUR 5 million per week, and Spohr conceded the Middle East loss is 'easily a 3-digit number.' Meanwhile the first quarter of 2026 still posted an adjusted operating loss of EUR 612 million (reported 6 May 2026), and full-year 2026 free cash flow is guided to only about EUR 0.9 billion against EUR 2.9 billion of net capital spending.

The structural handicaps are permanent and management says so. Asia only recovers when 'the Russian airspace reopens' — an event entirely outside its control, and Gulf and Chinese competitors keep the advantage until it happens. European and German location costs, taxes, fees and 'a very one-sided regulation from the European Union' (August 2025) ratchet one way. Spohr conceded to Bernstein in April 2025 that efficiency will not return to pre-COVID levels through the fleet transition — 'yes, there is an efficiency and cost impact.'

And the transition never ends. 2025 was 'a transition year'; 2026 'will have transitional elements'; the 8-10% margin destination is perpetually one fleet cycle away. On management's own telling the first clean year is 2027 — which means the buyer today is underwriting an 18-month wait, levered, into an unresolved oil shock.

What would confirm the bear: free cash flow missing the guided ~EUR 0.9 billion for 2026; the mid-single-digit margin guide cut at the 4 August 2026 half-year results; any Gulf re-escalation past the mid-August ceasefire expiry; or a further Boeing 787 delivery slip extending the efficiency drag into 2027. Note that our own peer work reaches the same verdict independently: against Air France-KLM, IAG and Ryanair, Lufthansa is 'the lowest-quality in the peer group' and 'the discount is fundamentally deserved.'
consensus_delta:
For a deep-value candidate the question is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into a company with stable or growing earnings power. Our honest answer is that it is not, and this is the crux of our pass: we cannot find the disagreement.

The street is Neutral — 19 analysts average a EUR 9.60 twelve-month target against a live price of EUR 9.12, with 7 buys, 8 holds and 4 sells. That is not a market looking the wrong way; that is a market that has looked, shrugged, and priced the name at roughly its parts. Our own sum-of-the-parts lands at EUR 8.75, i.e. slightly below where consensus and the tape already sit. When our independent work agrees with the street to within a few percent, there is no expectations arbitrage to harvest, and intellectual honesty requires saying so rather than manufacturing a delta.

Where we DO disagree is smaller than the thesis needs, and it cuts both ways. We think the market under-appreciates one thing: the low-cost-platform migration is contractual, permanent, and requires no negotiation. The 2023 pilots' agreement, as the chief executive described it in April 2025, 'allows us unlimited growth in Lufthansa City Airlines and in Discover' — the unions traded structural flexibility for salary, and Lufthansa is now quietly redirecting all growth to Discover, Edelweiss, City Airlines and ITA on an explicit return-on-capital rule (October 2025). That is a slow, unglamorous, genuinely undermodelled cost fix. Allegris at a 12% yield premium with roughly 95% of wide-bodies unconverted is a second undermodelled leg.

But we think the market over-appreciates something larger, and this is where we part company with the bulls rather than the bears. The entire street conversation on these calls was an income-statement conversation — unit revenue, margins, cargo, deliveries. Across all five calls, not one analyst asked when free cash flow turns positive, or how a rising dividend is funded from negative free cash flow with EUR 5.32 billion of net debt and an Altman Z-score of 1.2. The consensus is anchored on adjusted operating profit, which rose 19% in 2025 — and adjusted operating profit sits above the depreciation and interest of the very fleet programme that is the strategy. One line lower, net income has fallen three years running (EUR 1.67 billion to EUR 1.38 billion to EUR 1.34 billion) and earnings per share is down 2.6%. The street's implicit assumption that the adjusted-profit recovery is the shareholder's recovery has been wrong for three consecutive years and, on management's own guidance of a transitional 2026, will be wrong again this year.

So the delta is real but it points the wrong way for a long. The market is not too bearish on Lufthansa. If anything it is too willing to accept the adjusted measure as the true one. We are not paid to be right about that at EUR 9.12, because the parts already say EUR 8.75.
forcing_function:
For a deep-value name the forcing function must be an event that compels the market to re-rate — a buyback authorisation, an activist, an asset sale, a dividend initiation. Our finding is that Lufthansa has no such event ahead of it, and that this is the decisive fact in the case.

The two hard dates that existed have both passed. The ITA Airways majority option — genuinely the largest strategic lever available — was approved by the Supervisory Board on 12 May 2026 and announced on 13 May 2026 (41% to 90% for EUR 325 million), and exercised in June 2026. The dividend was approved on 12 May 2026, went ex on 13 May and was paid on 18 May 2026. Both are behind the tape. The ITA closing, expected in the first quarter of 2027 subject to European Commission and Department of Justice clearance, is a compliance milestone rather than a forcing function: the terms are fixed, the price is disclosed, and the market has had two months to price it. It also consumes EUR 325 million of cash from a balance sheet that is generating none.

The event that WOULD force a re-rating is precisely the one management has ruled out. A Lufthansa Technik minority stake sale or listing would crystallise the single most valuable part of our sum-of-the-parts — EUR 6.7 billion of the EUR 15.65 billion base-case enterprise value, sitting inside an airline multiple. That process was shelved in November 2023, and the company has since confirmed it remains sole shareholder and will grow Technik 'without the involvement of another shareholder.' Absent a change of heart there is no mechanism to surface that value; investors simply hold it at the airline's multiple indefinitely. There is no activist on the register, no strategic review, no governance reset, and no buyback authorisation. The Federal Republic of Germany's history with this asset makes an activist-forced breakup structurally unlikely.

What remains on the calendar is dated but not forcing. The half-year results on 4 August 2026 are the next hard date and the first real test of whether the maintained 2026 guidance (adjusted operating profit significantly above prior year, mid-single-digit margin, ~EUR 0.9 billion adjusted free cash flow) survives the EUR 1.7 billion fuel headwind. An earnings print is a test, not a catalyst — and its asymmetry runs against the buyer, since the guide is already in the consensus EUR 9.60 target while a cut would de-rate a distress-zone balance sheet. Around mid-August 2026 the US-Iran ceasefire clock expires; that is a dated macro binary that can only hurt this name.

The deeper problem is that the only genuine re-rating path is not an event at all — it is the arrival of positive free cash flow, and management's own guidance places the first clean year in 2027. The chief executive designated 2025 a transition year and conceded 2026 'will have transitional elements.' A thesis whose forcing function is 'the numbers eventually get better, probably next year' is not a special situation. It is a hope with a calendar attached.

The regime makes this worse, not better. Our current read rewards hard-dated, structural special situations — spinoffs, index-orphan forced flow, distressed deleveraging — and explicitly penalises catalysts that are past or out of window, which is exactly what Lufthansa's are. It also warns against theses hinging on a single shared macro factor, and Lufthansa's entire 2026 earnings bridge hinges on one: oil. That is the opposite of the resolution-driver independence the regime demands. Nothing here is orthogonal to anything.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months are unusually well-populated with ways to lose money before any payoff arrives, and for a deep-value name the question is whether something kills the thesis before the discount converges. Here, there is no discount to converge — so the near-term risks are pure cost.

The fuel hump is the dominant one and it is already quantified by management: an incremental EUR 1.7 billion fuel bill for 2026 from the Gulf spike, with only 80-83% of passenger-airline fuel hedged. Management's own framing on the March 2026 call was that the hedge is a relative advantage over unhedged American competitors — a relative advantage that still concedes EUR 1.7 billion in absolute terms. Worse, the chief financial officer flagged a timing mechanic that lands precisely in this window: the group settles 'the physical fuel bill with a month's delay,' so the spike passes into reported costs on a lag. The hedge also decays — an 80% hedge ratio is a 2026 fact, not a permanent one, and re-hedging at post-spike prices is how an oil shock becomes a 2027 cost base.

The cash-burn hump is structural and concurrent. Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is already negative EUR 390 million. Capital spending runs at 1.92 times depreciation and 109% of operating cash flow. For 2026 the company guides to about EUR 2.9 billion of net capital spending against only ~EUR 0.9 billion of adjusted free cash flow — and the first quarter of 2026 posted an adjusted operating loss of EUR 612 million (reported 6 May 2026). Airlines earn their year in the third quarter; if the summer disappoints, the full-year free-cash-flow guide is the first thing to go, and it is a guide with very little cushion.

The balance sheet gives that combination teeth. Net debt of EUR 5.32 billion, an Altman Z-score of 1.2 in the distress zone, negative EUR 4.2 billion of working capital and a current ratio of 0.81 mean Lufthansa does not have the balance sheet to absorb a bad summer gracefully. A dividend raised 10% out of negative free cash flow is the first discretionary item a stressed board revisits.

The macro headwinds are dated and they sit inside the window. The US-Iran 60-day ceasefire clock expires around mid-August 2026 — nine days after Lufthansa's half-year results — and it is more fragile than the headline suggests (a US airstrike on 26 June 2026 followed an alleged violation). Lufthansa still had ten destinations closed as of the March 2026 call at a stated EUR 5 million per week, and the chief executive conceded the Middle East loss is 'easily a 3-digit number.' Brent at roughly USD 71 is currently deflating, which is a genuine offset — but that cuts both ways: it means the market is currently pricing the benign oil path, so a re-escalation is an unpriced downside rather than a priced one. Meanwhile the Section 122 tariff expiry on 24 July 2026 is a live near-dated binary for the Technik parts flow, even though aircraft and aircraft parts have so far been carved out of the tariff schedule per the chief executive's August 2025 remarks.

And there is an execution tail management does not control: Boeing 787 deliveries have slipped repeatedly across these calls — from '9 to 10 aircraft by the end of the year' (April 2025) down to 'pretty optimistic to be above 6… 8 probably the most likely shot' (October 2025). Each slip extends the crew and maintenance inefficiency that the chief executive already conceded keeps the group 'a way from going to the same efficiency levels we have seen before COVID.'

The honest summary: the first dated test is the half-year results on 4 August 2026, and the risk there is asymmetric against the buyer. Beating a maintained guide moves the stock little because the guide is already in the EUR 9.60 consensus target; cutting the mid-single-digit margin guide or the ~EUR 0.9 billion free-cash-flow guide would be a genuine de-rating event into a distress-zone balance sheet.
positioning_washout:
There is no forced-selling dynamic to exploit here, and pretending otherwise would be the easiest way to manufacture a thesis that does not exist.

The mechanical question is whether a pivot or a dividend cut would force a yield-focused or passive shareholder base to liquidate. On the evidence, no such flush is set up. Management moved in the opposite direction: it RAISED the dividend 10% to EUR 0.33 per share for 2025, at a 30% payout ratio and roughly a 4% yield, and shareholders approved it at the 12 May 2026 Annual General Meeting. It was paid on 18 May 2026. A company that just raised its distribution and reaffirmed a positive full-year outlook (6 May 2026) is not about to trigger a yield-holder exodus in the next two quarters. If anything, the raise was designed to hold that shareholder base in place — the chief executive framed it explicitly as making sure 'shareholders already participate' in the improvement.

The positioning data we have shows an absence of pressure in either direction, which is the worst configuration for an event-driven buyer. The smart-money score is 28 out of 100 — institutional interest is low, but low and stable is not the same as capitulating. Institutional flow reads a perfectly neutral 50 out of 100: no accumulation, no distribution. The insider buy ratio is 0.00, meaning management has not bought a single share — notable for a team that has spent six quarters telling the market the turnaround is working, and a quiet argument against the mispricing thesis. If the people who know the EUR 1.5 billion turnaround programme best believed the stock were 40% cheap, the ratio would not be zero.

The technical posture confirms it: the stock trades 11% above its 200-day moving average and 69% up its 52-week range (EUR 6.72 to EUR 10.29), near the upper end after a run. This is not a washed-out, forced-seller tape — it is a name that has already recovered most of the way to its highs. Buying 69% up the range into a fired catalyst is the opposite of buying a flush.

And the one structural forced-seller mechanic the current regime favours is absent. Our regime read ranks forced-sellers and spinoffs as the fattest lane available — mechanical, price-insensitive, calendar-dated flow. Lufthansa offers none of it: no index-orphan stub, no distribution, no regulator-ordered divestiture, no parent overhang. The Lufthansa Technik minority sale that could have created exactly that kind of event was shelved in November 2023 and management confirms it remains sole shareholder.

The realistic washout scenario runs against us, not for us. If the 4 August 2026 half-year print cuts the free-cash-flow guide, the dividend becomes the visible casualty — a distribution funded from negative free cash flow on a distress-zone balance sheet — and the yield holders would then leave. That is a flush we would want to buy after, not before. It is also precisely the specific event a watchlist entry would wait for, and it is why we would rather own this name at EUR 6 than at EUR 9.12.
moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now. This is a good operational turnaround inside a bad investment at EUR 9.12, and the two things are not in conflict.

Let us be clear about what we are not saying. We are not saying management is failing — on the contrary, this is one of the more credible teams we have reviewed. They admitted the 2024 miss without spin ('we did fall short of our targets we had set ourselves for '24'), attributed 95% of it to their own core brand, promised operational stabilisation, and then delivered it in measurable euros: 99% regularity, punctuality up more than 10 points, and irregularity costs down 43% — 'equivalent of EUR 362 million.' The chief financial officer refused three separate invitations to bless a soft consensus number. The chief executive raised the Middle East damage himself rather than waiting to be asked. That earns a credibility score of 4, and it is genuinely earned.

The problem is that credibility is not the same as value, and the operational win has not reached the owner. Adjusted operating profit rose about 19% in 2025 — and net income fell for the third consecutive year (EUR 1.67 billion to EUR 1.38 billion to EUR 1.34 billion), with earnings per share down 2.6%. Both are true, and the reason is mechanical: the adjusted measure sits above the depreciation and interest of the record fleet programme that IS the strategy. Free cash flow is negative EUR 390 million on a trailing basis; capital spending is 109% of operating cash flow. The company is paying a 10%-raised dividend out of money it does not generate, against EUR 5.32 billion of net debt and an Altman Z-score of 1.2 in the distress zone. Four of our five valuation models return negative margins of safety because there is no cash to discount; only Graham's book-based measure shows a discount, and book value is the wrong lens on a business earning 0.4% on invested capital.

The sum-of-the-parts settles it. Valuing the pieces properly — Technik at a genuine aerospace multiple of 10x (EUR 6.7 billion), the passenger franchise at a mid-range 5x (EUR 7.0 billion), Cargo at 5x (EUR 1.25 billion), the 90% ITA stake at EUR 0.7 billion — gives an enterprise value of EUR 15.65 billion. Subtract EUR 5.32 billion of net debt and you get EUR 8.75 per share against a live price of EUR 9.12. There is no conglomerate discount here to harvest. The parts sum to roughly what the market already pays. Our peer work reached that conclusion independently ('the discount is fundamentally deserved'), and so did the street (Neutral, EUR 9.60 average target across 19 analysts). When our parts, our peers and the consensus all land within a few percent of the tape, the intellectually honest answer is that there is no edge — not that we should hunt harder for one.

On timing, the case is worse than merely fair value. Both load-bearing catalysts have already fired: the ITA majority option was board-approved on 12 May and announced 13 May 2026 (41% to 90% for EUR 325 million, closing expected in the first quarter of 2027), and the EUR 0.33 dividend went ex on 13 May and was paid on 18 May 2026. A buyer today gets neither. The one event that could crystallise the sum-of-the-parts — a Technik stake sale or listing, worth EUR 6.7 billion of our base-case enterprise value and currently trapped at an airline multiple — was shelved in November 2023 and management confirms it remains sole shareholder. There is no activist, no buyback, no strategic review, no forced flow. What is left is a soft, non-binding turnaround target (EUR 1.5 billion gross in 2026, EUR 2.5 billion by 2028) that has been restated on every call for six quarters, inside a rolling 'transition year' framing in which 2025 was transitional, 2026 has 'transitional elements,' and the first clean year is 2027 on management's own telling.

The regime makes us more negative, not less, and we let it move the call. Our current read rewards hard-dated structural special situations and explicitly penalises catalysts that are past or out of window — Lufthansa's are exactly that. It prizes resolution-driver independence and warns against theses hinging on one shared macro factor. Lufthansa's entire 2026 bridge hinges on precisely one: oil. Management guided to a EUR 1.7 billion incremental fuel bill with 80-83% hedged, settles the physical bill on a month's lag, and faces a US-Iran ceasefire clock expiring around mid-August 2026 — nine days after its half-year results. Brent at roughly USD 71 is deflating today, which means the benign path is the one already priced; the escalation is the unpriced tail. This thesis is orthogonal to nothing.

And there is no wash-out to buy. The stock trades 11% above its 200-day average and 69% up its 52-week range, with institutional flow a flat 50 out of 100 and an insider buy ratio of 0.00 — not one share bought by the people who know the turnaround best. That last fact deserves weight.

On the value score, judged purely on valuation versus our fair value and forensic quality, ignoring the fired catalyst and the regime entirely: a 4% premium to a properly-built sum-of-the-parts, negative free cash flow, 0.4% return on invested capital and a distress-zone solvency score is a 2. The catalyst-aware score is also a 2, and we want to be explicit that this is a coincidence of two independent readings rather than a default — the catalyst overlay is unambiguously negative (both events fired, oil-dependent, no forcing function), and the value case is separately absent because the price already equals the parts. Had the stock been at EUR 6, the value score would be a 4 while the catalyst score stayed at 2. It is not at EUR 6.

On the moat we resolve toward NARROW and STABLE rather than eroding, and this matters because it keeps Lufthansa out of value-trap territory. The franchise is real — hub slots at Frankfurt, Munich and Zurich, the antitrust-immunised North Atlantic joint venture with United and Air Canada, Miles & More, and Technik's scale position in a USD 100 billion market with an aging-fleet tailwind. Returns of 0.4% are low from a rebuilt base rather than high-and-falling: book value per share compounds at 12.7% over five years and the company is emerging from a EUR 2.19 billion loss in 2021. The secular threat is manageable, not terminal — IATA projects passenger numbers doubling over 20 years against constrained supply, and Lufthansa's own data shows premium demand outrunning economy ('first class is even going better than business class'). No structural force is melting this base, so no cap binds. Lufthansa is not a value trap. It is simply fully priced.

What would change our mind, specifically. A price near EUR 6-6.50 — around the 52-week low and a genuine discount to the parts — would make the value case a 4 on the same facts. A cut to the ~EUR 0.9 billion free-cash-flow guide on 4 August 2026 would likely deliver that price, and that is the flush to wait for. Alternatively, a revived Lufthansa Technik stake sale or listing would be a true forcing function and would re-rate the whole enterprise; we would move immediately on that announcement. Absent one of those, we are being asked to pay full fair value for a levered, negative-cash-flow airline whose catalysts have already fired, whose earnings bridge depends on the oil price, and whose own management says the first clean year is 2027. We would rather wait and be wrong about the last 5% than own the balance sheet through the summer.
sop_fair_value: EUR 8.75 per share (base case; reconciled range EUR 8.60-8.90) — approximately 4% below the live price of EUR 9.12.
sop_breakdown:
Base-case parts, blending the favourable and adverse cases toward the middle: Passenger Airlines at 5.0x on EUR 1.4 billion of segment operating profit = EUR 7.0 billion; Lufthansa Technik at 10.0x on EUR 670 million = EUR 6.7 billion; Lufthansa Cargo at 5.0x on EUR 250 million = EUR 1.25 billion; the 90% ITA Airways stake at EUR 0.7 billion. That sums to an enterprise value of EUR 15.65 billion. Subtracting net debt of EUR 5.32 billion (ex-lease basis, recomputed from the 31 March 2026 balance sheet: EUR 13.02 billion of borrowings less EUR 7.70 billion of cash) leaves EUR 10.33 billion of equity across 1.202 billion shares — about EUR 8.59 per share. We round the base to EUR 8.75 to credit two small, real options the arithmetic ignores: the possible refund of the Technik tariffs the chief executive flagged as 'ruled illegal by the Supreme Court' in March 2026, and the unconverted ~95% of the wide-body fleet still to receive the Allegris cabin that is already earning a 12% yield premium.

The conclusion the parts deliver is the important one: Lufthansa's businesses sum to roughly what the market is already paying. There is no conglomerate discount to harvest here. The two genuinely good assets — Technik at EUR 6.7 billion and the hub/joint-venture passenger franchise — are already carrying the whole equity value, and the EUR 5.32 billion of net debt consumes a third of the enterprise. Sensitivity is dominated by the passenger multiple: each additional turn of EV/EBIT on the Passenger Airlines segment is worth about EUR 1.16 per share, which is why the bull and bear cases sit so far apart on an unchanged asset base.
risk_reward: Unattractive: the base-case sum-of-the-parts (EUR 8.75) sits about 4% BELOW the live price of EUR 9.12, so there is no upside to fair value to speak of, against an adverse case of EUR 5.50. In levels: downside to the adverse case is roughly EUR 3.62 per share; upside to base-case fair value is negative (roughly EUR 0.37 of downside), and upside to the favourable case is EUR 3.88 per share but requires a full turnaround plus a re-rating of the passenger multiple to IAG-like levels. There is no structural floor beneath the stock — no net cash (this is a net-debt business), no deal terms, no tender. The 4% dividend yield is explicitly NOT a floor, and neither is the EUR 6.72 52-week low. An investor is paying full sum-of-the-parts value for a business with negative free cash flow and a distress-zone solvency score, and being compensated only if the favourable case lands.
peer_comps_note:
Our peer work reaches the same conclusion as our own sum-of-the-parts, independently, which raises our confidence in the pass.

Against the true peer set — Air France-KLM, IAG (British Airways/Iberia), easyJet, Wizz Air, Ryanair and the US carriers — Lufthansa is, in our peer file's words, 'the lowest-quality in the peer group,' and 'the discount is fundamentally deserved.' The evidence is unambiguous: IAG earns roughly 10% on invested capital and Ryanair the highest returns and margins in European aviation, while Lufthansa earns 0.4% on invested capital, 3.4% net margin, and negative free cash flow, with an Altman Z-score of 1.19 in the distress zone. The peer verdict is 'in_line' — meaning Lufthansa is trading about where its quality says it should, not at an anomalous discount to be arbitraged.

The file carries no peer_override or anchor_multiple, so we set the passenger multiple from the observable European legacy range rather than from memory: roughly 4-6x enterprise-value-to-operating-profit, with Air France-KLM at the low end and IAG at the high end. We anchor our base case at 5.0x — deliberately mid-range, not at IAG's multiple, because Lufthansa has not earned IAG's returns. Our favourable case at 6.0x is the explicit assumption that it eventually does; that assumption, not the asset base, is what the bull case is really buying.

One cross-check matters. The Graham margin of safety of +84% is the only measure in our scan showing Lufthansa as cheap, and our peer note flags precisely why it should be discounted: it is a book-value measure, and 'cheap on Graham but structurally inferior to Ryanair and IAG.' Lufthansa's book value compounds (12.7% over five years) while its returns on that book sit near zero. Paying below book for assets earning 0.4% is not a bargain. The four cash-based models in our own scan (discounted cash flow, earnings power value, owner earnings, and the 15% intrinsic-value model) all return negative margins of safety — the models agree with each other and disagree with Graham, and on a business with negative free cash flow the cash-based models are the ones to believe.

External analyst opinion corroborates rather than contradicts: consensus across 19 analysts is Neutral with an average 12-month target of about EUR 9.60 (high EUR 21.00, low EUR 6.60), roughly 5% above the live EUR 9.12; a narrower 10-analyst set from the past three months averages about EUR 8.21, below the current price. The street, our peers, and our parts all land in the same place — this is priced.
interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — Deutsche Lufthansa AG (LHA.DE)

*Prepared for the investment committee. Sources: five consecutive Lufthansa Group earnings calls (6 March 2025 full-year 2024; 29 April 2025 first-quarter 2025; 1 August 2025 second-quarter 2025; 30 October 2025 third-quarter 2025; 6 March 2026 full-year 2025), the screener's financial trajectory, and dated public filings verified on 16 July 2026. Price used throughout: EUR 9.12 per share on XETRA (live quote, 16 July 2026).*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management tells has been remarkably consistent across these five calls, and that consistency is itself the most useful finding: for six straight quarters, the pitch has been *"the core airline is being fixed, and everything else is already working."*

**The opening position (March 2025).** Chief executive Carsten Spohr opened the full-year 2024 call by conceding a miss outright — "we did fall short of our targets we had set ourselves for '24" — and localised the damage with unusual precision: of the group's roughly EUR 1 billion decline in adjusted operating profit (adjusted EBIT, the company's preferred profit measure, which strips out one-off items), "more or less 95%, EUR 950 million were driven by Lufthansa Airline, our core brand." The rest of the portfolio was presented as the proof of concept for the multi-brand strategy: SWISS above EUR 800 million, Eurowings above EUR 200 million, Austrian EUR 76 million, Brussels a record EUR 60 million, Lufthansa Technik (the maintenance, repair and overhaul arm, known as MRO) a record EUR 635 million, and Lufthansa Cargo EUR 251 million. Spohr's framing was pointed: the group made EUR 1.6 billion "without a single euro contribution from the core airline."

**The through-line.** Across every subsequent call the same three pillars recur, in the same order: (1) operational stability first, financial recovery second; (2) fleet renewal and the new Allegris premium cabin as the yield engine; (3) the ITA Airways acquisition as the internationalisation milestone. Nothing was quietly dropped. That is a genuine mark in management's favour — many turnaround stories rotate their drivers when one fails to land.

**What expanded.** Two threads grew materially over the period. First, *operational stability* moved from aspiration to delivered metric: by October 2025 Spohr could report regularity at 99% and departure punctuality "improved by more than 10 percentage points," and by March 2026 the financial translation was quantified — flight irregularity costs down 43%, "equivalent of EUR 362 million." That is the single most credible number in the whole transcript set, because it is specific, cash-relevant, and repeatedly reconciled. Second, *ancillary revenue* (fees for bags, seat selection and upgrades) was introduced almost casually in April 2025 (up 18% year-on-year) and by March 2026 had become a headline driver, with Allegris commanding "12% higher yields for Allegris than for the former business class."

**What contracted.** The Asia narrative shrank steadily — from a growth region, to a capacity-discipline story, to an explicit structural handicap. By March 2026 the honest admission was that Asia only recovers when "the Russian airspace reopens," an event entirely outside management's control. China quietly disappeared as the second-largest intercontinental region and was replaced by India.

**The new shock (March 2026).** The most recent call opened not with the centenary celebration management had planned but with a Gulf conflict: ten destinations closed, a fuel-price spike, aircraft and crews repatriated early. Spohr's framing was characteristically two-sided — he pivoted within minutes to the hedging advantage ("we are hedged higher towards our main competitors") and to extra sections flown to Asia and South Africa on the freed-up aircraft. This is the tell of a management team that has learned to sell resilience during a crisis, and it is worth watching for exactly that reason.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

This is where the story and the numbers part company. The operational claims hold up well. The claim that this operational progress is producing shareholder value does not — at least not yet.

| Management claim | Quarter | What the financials show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Revenues increased by 6% to EUR 37.6 billion. That marks a new record." | Q4-24 call | Confirmed: revenue 35.44B (2023) → 37.58B (2024) → 39.60B (2025), +5.4% year-on-year, 3-year compound growth +8.6% | **Matches.** Top line is real and at a record. |
| Irregularity costs reduced 43%, "equivalent of EUR 362 million" | Q4-25 call | Consistent with adjusted EBIT rising ~19% in 2025 (EUR 1.645B → ~EUR 1.96B) | **Matches.** The most verifiable claim in the set. |
| "We have initiated a turnaround… which already led to significant improvements also on the financial side" | Q4-24 call, repeated throughout | Net income: **1.67B (2023) → 1.38B (2024) → 1.34B (2025)**. Earnings per share: 1.40 → 1.15 → **1.12, down 2.6% year-on-year**. Return on equity **0.2%**, return on invested capital **0.4%** | **Diverges sharply.** Three consecutive years of *declining* net income and earnings per share against a rising top line and a rising adjusted operating profit. The adjusted measure is improving; the number that belongs to shareholders is not. |
| Fleet renewal is the value engine — "the biggest fleet renewal of our company's history" | Q3-25 call | Free cash flow **negative**: trailing-twelve-month free cash flow **−EUR 390 million**; capital spending is **1.92× depreciation** and **109% of operating cash flow**; net capital spending guided to ~EUR 2.9 billion for 2026 | **The story is poorer than it sounds.** The fleet renewal is consuming every euro the business generates and then some. This is the mechanical reason adjusted EBIT can rise 19% while earnings per share falls: higher depreciation and interest on the new fleet sit below the adjusted line. |
| Lufthansa Technik "delivering once again a record level… adjusted EBIT" | Q2-25 call | Group gross margin **9.5% and contracting**; net margin only **3.4%** | **Partly matches.** Technik's own profit is real, but management conceded in Q4-25 that Technik "was suffering… under tariffs" and margin compressed in 2025. The MRO margin recovery to a 10% target by 2030 is an ambition, not a delivered trend. |
| "We are hedged higher towards our main competitors" — a relative fuel advantage | Q4-25 call | Verified externally: 80–83% of passenger-airline fuel hedged for 2026, but the company still guided to a **EUR 1.7 billion incremental fuel bill for 2026** | **True but insufficient.** A hedge that still admits EUR 1.7 billion of headwind is a speed bump, not a shield. |
| Balance sheet implicitly sound; dividend raised 10% | Q4-25 call | Net debt **EUR 5.32 billion** (ex-lease, recomputed from the 31 March 2026 balance sheet: EUR 13.02B borrowings less EUR 7.70B cash). **Altman Z-score 1.2** — the distress zone. Current ratio 0.81; working capital **−EUR 4.2 billion** | **Diverges.** Management is paying a rising dividend and funding a record fleet programme out of negative free cash flow, with a solvency score in the distress band. |
| Piotroski score 8/9 (accounting quality) | Screener | Genuinely strong — profitable, positive operating cash flow, improving margins on several legs | **Green.** The accounting quality is not the problem. The *cash* is. |

**The central forensic finding:** Lufthansa's narrative is built entirely on *adjusted EBIT*, a measure that sits above the depreciation and interest generated by the very fleet programme management calls its strategic centrepiece. Move one line down the income statement and the three-year trend reverses from "up 19%" to "down for three straight years." Both facts are true. Only one is in the headline.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Rising — but rising from a confessed low, and rising on operational rather than financial ground.**

- **Q4-24 (March 2025) — contrite but forward-leaning.** "A year filled with ups and downs"; the 2024 miss admitted without hedging. Yet Spohr signalled the turn: the fourth quarter was "by far the strongest quarter in the reporting period." Confidence: *low base, upward slope.*
- **Q1-25 (April 2025) — cautiously offensive.** "Record sales for the first time going above EUR 8 billion." Early defensive notes appear: "we're beginning to see early signs of some softness in the third quarter." Notably, management pre-empted rather than concealed this. Confidence: *rising, with hedges.*
- **Q2-25 (August 2025) — confident, with a new grievance.** "Operationally very stable, economically on track." But a defensive theme enters and never leaves: "the competitive disadvantage tied to location cost in our European home markets is becoming increasingly evident… constantly rising taxes and fees, and a very one-sided regulation from the European Union." Confidence: *high on execution, defensive on structure.*
- **Q3-25 (October 2025) — the most confident call in the set.** "Summer '25 clearly marked a turning point." Spohr's "endless summer" riff — "one day summer will last until Christmas" — is a man enjoying himself. Confidence: *peak.*
- **Q4-25 (March 2026) — confident under fire.** A war, a fuel spike and ten closed destinations, and the tone stays constructive: "my optimism continues." Spohr volunteers the Middle East question himself — "I was waiting for that question all morning because the Middle East being taken away from us has a huge impact on profitability for us" — and quantifies it as "easily a 3-digit number." Confidence: *steady; notably, he raised the bad news rather than waiting to be asked.*

**Offensive-to-defensive shift:** partial and specific. Growth language never left, but a durable defensive vocabulary took root from Q2-25 onward around three things management cannot control: German and EU location costs, Russian airspace closure, and now Gulf geopolitics. Management is increasingly explicit that its ceiling is set by others.

**Guidance specificity over time: improving.** The March 2025 call gave a vague "double-digit EBIT growth" that Jefferies' Jaina Mistry immediately and correctly attacked as meaningless ("double-digit can give you a wide range… are you comfortable with consensus EBIT on EUR 1.9 billion?"). By March 2026 and the Q1-2026 update, the guidance had hardened into a mid-single-digit adjusted operating margin, ~EUR 0.9 billion adjusted free cash flow and ~EUR 2.9 billion net capital spending. That is a real improvement in disclosure discipline.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: Medium-High.** Management delivers what it *operationally* promises and is honest when it misses. It has a persistent habit of framing every year as transitional.

**The track record across these calls:**

| Guided | When | Delivered? |
|---|---|---|
| 2024 targets | pre-March-2025 | **Missed** — admitted plainly: "we did fall short of our targets." Credit for candour; the miss is still a miss. |
| "Double-digit" 2025 adjusted EBIT growth | March 2025 | **Delivered.** 2025 adjusted EBIT rose ~19% (EUR 1.645B → ~EUR 1.96B), "a delta of EUR 350 million." Inside the guided range, if at the lower half of what "double-digit" could have implied. |
| EUR 1.5 billion gross turnaround contribution in 2026, rising to EUR 2.5 billion by 2028 | March 2025, reaffirmed | **In progress — the key open item.** The 2026 leg is the one the committee must underwrite. |
| Operational stabilisation | March 2025 | **Over-delivered.** Regularity 99%, punctuality +8 to +10 points, irregularity costs −43% (EUR 362 million). |
| 787 deliveries: "9 to 10 aircraft by the end of the year, fully usable" | April 2025 | **Missed, but not their fault.** By October 2025 the number had softened to "pretty optimistic to be above 6… 8 probably the most likely shot." Management flagged the Boeing/Collins/FAA dependency honestly and repeatedly. |
| 2026 outlook maintained despite the Gulf shock | Q1-2026 (6 May 2026) | **Held.** Adjusted EBIT still guided "significantly above prior year" with a mid-single-digit margin, absorbing the EUR 1.7 billion fuel headwind. Not yet tested. |

**Reconciling with the beat rate.** The screener records beats in 4 of the last 7 quarters (57%) — mediocre, and consistent with a team that guides honestly rather than sandbagging. **There is no sandbagging pattern here.** Chief financial officer Till Streichert explicitly refused the invitation to validate a soft consensus number ("let me not comment on the consensus. I think I've provided adequate components"). That is the opposite of a management team steering the street low so it can step over the bar.

**The one credibility scar — the rolling transition year.** In April 2025 Spohr called 2025 "a transition year to a certain degree, even '26 will have traditional [transitional] elements." In August 2025: "this year remains a transition year." In October 2025: efficiency gains arrive "starting in '26." In March 2026: 2025 was "a transition year, as you might recall, we have called [it] from the very beginning." The full-margin destination — Spohr's "8% to 10% margins" — has been perpetually one fleet cycle away. Management has now been explicit that 2025 *and* 2026 carry transitional drag, meaning the first clean year on their own telling is 2027.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**The recurring deflection — unit revenue.** Barclays' Andrew Lobbenberg pushed repeatedly on RASK (revenue per available seat kilometre — the airline industry's core pricing metric). Spohr's answer in Q4-25: "We don't guide on RASK, Andrew, and you know that." Streichert then engaged on definitions rather than direction, explaining that the reported −2% RASK "includes ancillaries, cargo revenues and also the revenue benefit from less [irregularity] events" while the regional RASK in the appendix excludes all three. That is a real and material disclosure point: **the headline unit-revenue figure is flattered by items that are not ticket pricing.** Analysts noticed. Management did not volunteer a clean like-for-like pricing trend.

**The question that became bad news.** Bernstein's Alex Irving asked in April 2025 whether Lufthansa was over-crewed: "it looks like you've got more employees in the airlines now despite lower production." Spohr rejected the framing but conceded the substance completely — "we will be… a way from going to the same efficiency levels we have seen before COVID with all these new aircraft entering… yes, there is an efficiency and cost impact." Irving's question was the right one, and the answer was an admission that structural cost inefficiency persists through at least 2026. This is the pressure point that most directly explains why record revenue is not reaching the bottom line.

**What analysts worry about that management is not addressing.** Nobody on these calls asked the question this committee must ask: *when does free cash flow turn positive, and how is a rising dividend funded from negative free cash flow while net debt sits at EUR 5.32 billion and the Altman Z-score is 1.2?* Analysts pressed on margins, RASK, cargo and deliveries — all income-statement questions. The cash-conversion and balance-sheet question went unasked across all five calls. Management, understandably, did not raise it.

**The non-answer worth noting.** Jefferies' Mistry, twice, tried to get Streichert to bless the EUR 1.9 billion 2025 consensus. He declined both times. In hindsight the actual ~EUR 1.96 billion means he *would* have been right to bless it — his refusal was discipline, not evasion.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

**🔴 Red flags**

- **The bottom line has gone backwards for three years while the narrative went forwards.** Net income 1.67B → 1.38B → 1.34B (2023–2025); earnings per share 1.40 → 1.15 → 1.12. Every call in this set was delivered against a *falling* earnings trend. (All five quarters.)
- **Free cash flow is negative and structurally so.** Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow −EUR 390 million; capital spending 1.92× depreciation. The fleet programme management sells as the future is the reason the present generates no cash. (Q3-25, Q4-25 fleet discussion vs financials.)
- **A dividend raised 10% out of negative free cash flow**, with a solvency score in the distress band (Altman Z 1.2) and a 30% payout ratio computed on earnings that are themselves declining. (Q4-25.)
- **The rolling "transition year."** Three consecutive years in which the clean year is next year. (Q1-25, Q2-25, Q3-25, Q4-25.)
- **Headline unit revenue is flattered by non-ticket items** — ancillaries, cargo belly and irregularity-cost relief are all inside the reported RASK. (Q3-25, Streichert.)
- **Structural handicaps are now permanent narrative furniture**: Russian airspace, EU regulation, German location costs. Management has, in effect, told the market its ceiling is set by third parties. (Q2-25 onward.)
- **Persistent overstaffing conceded**, with efficiency deferred past 2026. (Q1-25, Spohr to Bernstein.)

**🟢 Green flags**

- **Operational turnaround delivered and quantified**: regularity 99%, punctuality +10 points, irregularity cost −43% / EUR 362 million. This is the rarest thing in a turnaround — a promise made, kept, and measured in euros. (Q3-25, Q4-25.)
- **Candour about failure.** The 2024 miss was volunteered, attributed (95% to the core brand), and not spun. The Middle East hit was raised by the chief executive unprompted. (Q4-24, Q4-25.)
- **The non-airline portfolio genuinely works.** Technik EUR 635 million (record) and Cargo EUR 251 million in 2024, with the group earning EUR 1.6 billion "without a single euro contribution from the core airline." The multi-brand, multi-hub structure is validated, not merely asserted. (Q4-24.)
- **Allegris is producing measurable pricing power**: "12% higher yields for Allegris than for the former business class," ancillaries +15% in 2025, with only 10 of ~200 wide-bodies converted at mid-2025 — a long runway that is arithmetic, not hope. (Q2-25, Q4-25.)
- **Guidance discipline improved** from "double-digit" hand-waving to explicit margin, free-cash-flow and capital-spending figures.
- **Accounting quality is high** (Piotroski 8/9); revenue at a record EUR 39.6 billion; book value per share compounding at 12.7% over five years.
- **ITA was accretive earlier than promised** — "earlier than expected, we see positive financial effects from our investment in ITA already in the second quarter," with the 41% stake contributing EUR 90 million of net income in 2025. (Q2-25, Q4-25.)

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The capital-allocation vocabulary hardened — and it is the most important shift in the set.** In October 2025 Spohr answered a routine capacity question with an unusually disciplined formulation: "since coming out of COVID, beyond operational requirements, we really allocate aircraft and growth according to ROCE principle. So where do we return investments highest?" He then named the beneficiaries — Discover, Edelweiss, Lufthansa City Airlines, ITA — every one of them a *lower-cost* platform, and none of them the core Lufthansa mainline. He added that this is "also internally clearly communicated to unions, to our staff."

Read plainly: **Lufthansa is systematically starving its own flag carrier of growth and redirecting it to cheaper labour platforms, and is saying so publicly to pressure the unions.** The April 2025 call made the mechanism explicit — the 2023 pilots' contract "allows us unlimited growth in Lufthansa City Airlines and in Discover… they decided in '23 to rather go for high salary increases. And on the other hand, for that, we got the freedom to use growth in those airlines." This is a slow, contractual, structural cost fix that does not depend on winning a fight. It is the single most underappreciated positive in these transcripts.

**"Transition year" is doing load-bearing work.** The phrase is not decoration; it is the mechanism by which a three-year earnings decline is presented as progress.

**Competition talk shifted from carriers to states.** Early calls benchmark against airlines. Later calls benchmark against jurisdictions — Gulf carriers' airspace access, EU regulation, German taxation. Management's competitive frame has moved from "we can beat them" to "the playing field is tilted."

**A quiet geographic re-basing.** "Second largest intercontinental area for Lufthansa is not anymore China but by now India" (Q4-25), alongside an Air India partnership. China was dropped without ceremony.

**The tariff reversal is a real, unmodelled positive.** In Q4-25 Spohr noted the US tariffs that cost Technik roughly EUR 20 million in the first half of 2025 "have been ruled illegal by the Supreme Court. So at least they don't go forward. Probably there will also be reimbursements." A margin headwind is becoming a possible one-off tailwind.

**One voice, one message.** No management change across the period; Spohr and Streichert have been consistent and mutually reinforcing. There is no new voice saying anything different — which removes a common source of narrative drift, and also removes any fresh perspective.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE.**

Not STRENGTHENING, despite a strong temptation to call it that. The operational recovery is genuine, measured and delivered — but it has now run for six quarters without reaching the bottom line. Net income has fallen three years running, earnings per share is down 2.6% year-on-year, free cash flow is negative, and return on invested capital is 0.4%. A turnaround that improves adjusted operating profit by 19% while the owner's earnings decline is not yet strengthening the enterprise; it is offsetting the cost of the fleet transition. Not DETERIORATING either — revenue is at a record, accounting quality is high, the balance sheet is stressed but not breaking, and the operational fix is real.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing a position:**

**Every euro of the operational recovery is currently being consumed by the fleet programme, and the company is paying a rising dividend out of negative free cash flow while carrying EUR 5.32 billion of net debt and an Altman Z-score of 1.2.** The bull case is not "does the turnaround work" — it demonstrably is working operationally. The bull case is "does the turnaround out-earn the capital intensity before the balance sheet or the cycle forces a choice." Management's own answer is that 2026 still carries transitional drag and 2027 is the first clean year — while a EUR 1.7 billion fuel headwind lands in 2026 and a Gulf conflict remains unresolved. The director is not underwriting an operational thesis. The director is underwriting a *cash-conversion* thesis, on a levered balance sheet, into a live oil shock, with the company's own guidance putting the payoff a year beyond the current fiscal year.

**Economic moat: NARROW.**

The moat type is a *regulatory-license and scale-cost* hybrid: slot portfolios at Frankfurt, Munich and Zurich; a six-hub European network; the Miles & More loyalty franchise; the North Atlantic joint venture with United and Air Canada (an antitrust-immunised structure that is genuinely hard to replicate); and, distinctly, Lufthansa Technik's intangible/scale position in a global MRO market management sizes at roughly USD 100 billion a year with a structural aging-fleet tailwind.

The width judgement is set by the returns evidence, not the asset list. **Return on invested capital of 0.4% and return on equity of 0.2% are far below any plausible cost of capital**, gross margin is 9.5% and contracting, and net margin is 3.4%. A business earning 0.4% on invested capital does not have a wide moat regardless of how attractive its slots are. But the returns are *low from a rebuilt base*, not *high and falling*: book value per share has compounded at 12.7% over five years, adjusted operating profit rose 19% in 2025, and the company is emerging from a 2021 loss of EUR 2.19 billion. That is the signature of a narrow moat at a cyclical and transitional low, not an eroding one.

**Moat trend: STABLE.** Two forces offset. Eroding it: the Russian-airspace handicap versus Gulf and Chinese carriers is a genuine, unrecoverable structural cost disadvantage on Asian routes; European regulatory and location costs rise on a one-way ratchet; Ryanair, Wizz and easyJet continue to compress short-haul economics. Widening it: the low-cost-platform migration (Discover, City Airlines, Edelweiss, ITA) is contractually secured and permanent; Allegris is demonstrating 12% pricing uplift with roughly 95% of the wide-body fleet still unconverted; Technik grows above a market compounding at 2–3%; and the ITA majority acquisition adds a sixth hub and doubles Latin American reach. Net: stable.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE — and the cheapness is neither a clean fear-print nor a value trap.**

No structural force threatens aviation's terminal value. The demand curve is the opposite of secular decline: management cites IATA's forecast that global passenger numbers double over the next 20 years against constrained aircraft supply — "strong demand growth meets limited supply very likely for many years to come." None of the recognised terminal-impairment forces applies here. Artificial intelligence does not displace physical travel; the videoconferencing thesis was tested to destruction in 2020–2021 and premium long-haul demand is now running ahead of economy on Lufthansa's own data ("first class is even going better than business class, business class is going better than premium economy"). The energy transition is a cost and regulatory drag on aviation, not a demand-displacement force — there is no substitute technology for long-haul flight on any relevant horizon.

The honest characterisation of the discount is therefore neither of the two clean answers. It is **a deserved quality discount, not a mispricing**. Lufthansa is cheap on book-value and Graham measures precisely because it converts almost none of its record revenue into owner cash: negative free cash flow, 0.4% return on invested capital, a distress-zone solvency score, and a cost structure that is politically and contractually hard to move. That is not the market pricing in terminal decline against stable earnings power — the earnings power genuinely is impaired today, by the company's own admission, through at least 2026. The base is cyclical and recovering, not melting; but the market is not making an error that requires correcting. It is charging a fair price for a low-return, high-capital-intensity, geopolitically-levered business that happens to own two genuinely good assets (Technik and the hub/joint-venture franchise) inside a mediocre one.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 4 | TRAJECTORY: STABLE | MOAT: NARROW | MOAT_TREND: STABLE | SECULAR_THREAT: manageable
